catalog_quote: In this section I have looked at pitch in disyllabic words. The data show that there are three different word tone systems in the Tibetan languages studied here: tone template, word tone, and syllable tone. In the tone template languages (Dolpo and Mugom Tibetan), the four monosyllabic patterns are reduced to two disyllabic pitch patterns, and these patterns are derived from the register of the first syllable. The first syllable carries the contrastive pitch, and the non-initial syllable exhibits the predetermined characteristics of the template rather than its inherent or underlying characteristics.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mugom is analysed as a word-tone ('tone template') language: the high/low register (and level/falling) contrast is carried by the first syllable of the word only; non-initial syllables take a fixed template pitch (in the Dolpo data, high falling) regardless of their citation-form pitch, and the tonal domain is at most two syllables. The paper formulates no rule for word stress in Mugom; the word 'stress' occurs only in the Dolpo (p. 34-35) and Lhomi (pp. 40-43) discussions.
new_statements.exceptions: Sec. 6.1.2 is headed 'Dolpo Tibetan (and Mugom)' but its Table 12, Figures 17-18 and text are Dolpo; the p. 35 line 'a helpful auditory clue is listening for a perceived stress on the second syllable (high register) and a jump up in pitch to the second syllable (low register)' is a transcription heuristic for the two-way disyllabic template and is not attributed to Mugom data. Trisyllabic/quadrisyllabic compounds (Dolpo data) split into two-syllable tonal domains (sec. 6.1.3).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (mono- and disyllabic citation forms elicited from a Mugu-village speaker; pitch tracks of isolated words). Compounds and longer words only touched on for Dolpo.
new_statements.identity_note: Watters 2002 (fn. 2, p. 1) describes 'the variety of Mugom.. of Mugu village, Mugu district of West Nepal', i.e. Mugom proper (Mugugaun-Mugali), not the Karmarong/Karani variety; both fall under Glottolog mugo1238 / ISO muk (Ethnologue 'Mugom-Karmarong'; Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 use 'Karmarong (Mugu)' for the whole group). The paper's stress remarks (pp. 34-35) belong to the Dolpo data (dolp1239), not Mugom.

sources.note: Mugu / Karmarong appear only in geography and classification (p. 81; sec. 9.8.2 SW-section group 'Karmarong (Mugu)'; population figures). Sec. 7.3.3 'Stress' (pp. 241-242) is family-level (stress distinctive mainly in Balti; secondary in Lhasa, mBalhag) and 7.3.4 'Prosodic patterns' gives a trochaic (strong-weak) pattern for tonal/register dialects in general. Nothing Mugom-specific.
